case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Takings Clause scrutiny for permit exactions under Nollan/Dolan (as extended in Koontz to monetary exactions) applies when the exaction is a generally applicable, legislatively set impact fee rather than an ad hoc, discretionary permit condition.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Fifth Amendment Takings Clause (as incorporated against the States via the Fourteenth Amendment), specifically the unconstitutional-conditions doctrine as applied to land-use permit exactions.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Sheetz argues that the County’s traffic impact fee is a monetary exaction imposed as a condition of receiving a building permit and therefore must satisfy the heightened Nollan/Dolan standards (essential nexus and rough proportionality), regardless of whether the fee was imposed through a generally applicable legislative schedule; otherwise governments can evade constitutional limits by labeling exactions “legislative” and imposing broadly applicable fees untethered to the impacts of the particular project.
case_analysis.respondent_position: El Dorado County argues that Nollan/Dolan/Koontz are limited to ad hoc, individualized, discretionary permit conditions and do not apply to legislatively prescribed, generally applicable development fees; instead, such fees are governed by California’s statutory “reasonable relationship” framework (the Mitigation Fee Act), and extending Nollan/Dolan to broadly applicable fees would constitutionalize routine cost-spreading policy judgments traditionally left to legislatures.
key_precedents: Koontz v. St. Johns River Water Management District (2013)
San Remo Hotel L.P. v. City & County of San Francisco (Cal. 2002)
Usery v. Turner Elkhorn Mining Co. (1976)
San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court (Cal. 1996)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent contention—that generally applicable, legislatively set impact fees are effectively taxes and should avoid Nollan/Dolan in favor of deferential due-process review—has real force as an administrability and federalism concern, because we should be wary of turning federal courts into rate-setters for local land-use finance. But as Justice Kagan stresses, Koontz’s unconstitutional-conditions logic is about permit leverage over a specific property owner, and that coercive dynamic is not categorically cured by moving the demand from an administrator to an ordinance; a legislative carveout would invite straightforward evasion by relabeling identical exactions. I agree with Justice Thomas that the Takings Clause does not textually distinguish legislative from administrative exactions, yet I would write narrowly: Nollan/Dolan may apply to monetary exactions imposed as permit conditions even when authorized by legislation, while leaving for as-applied cases how “rough proportionality” operates for broadly applicable fee schedules and recognizing that state-law schemes may often satisfy the constitutional floor. That preserves precedent and institutional legitimacy without creating a manipulable loophole that would hollow out Koontz.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that generally applicable, legislatively set impact fees are mere taxes or economic regulation outside Nollan/Dolan—fails as a matter of text and original public meaning: the Takings Clause does not create a legislative safe harbor for extracting property without just compensation through permit conditions. Chief Justice Roberts is right that a categorical exemption for legislatively authorized fees would provide an obvious roadmap for evasion, effectively nullifying Koontz’s application of Nollan/Dolan to monetary exactions by simple relabeling. Justice Gorsuch’s point reinforces the proper focus: the constitutional injury is the government’s leveraging of the permitting power over a specific owner and parcel, not the identity of the decisionmaker. Administrability and reliance interests may counsel a narrow holding and may bear on evidentiary showings of nexus and rough proportionality, but they cannot displace the federal constitutional floor.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that generally applicable, legislatively set impact fees resemble taxes or user fees and that applying Nollan/Dolan could entangle federal courts in local fiscal policy. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Koontz is centrally about permit leverage and unconstitutional conditions, and a categorical legislative carveout would invite straightforward evasion by re-labeling the same exactions in ordinances. Justice Thomas’s textual point reinforces that nothing in the Takings Clause makes heightened scrutiny turn on the identity of the decisionmaker; general applicability may go to how the government proves nexus and rough proportionality, not whether constitutional scrutiny is triggered. I therefore remain with petitioner, favoring a narrow holding that preserves administrability without creating an atextual loophole.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—administrability and democratic accountability for generally applicable, legislatively set fees—has force, because we should not turn federal courts into zoning finance boards. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, a categorical “legislative” carveout would be an obvious roadmap for evasion: the same coercive permit leverage over a specific applicant and parcel could be replicated by ordinance, draining Nollan/Dolan/Koontz of practical protection for ordinary owners who cannot realistically litigate. Koontz’s logic is about unconstitutional conditions and leverage, not the identity of the decisionmaker or whether the exaction is framed as money versus land, so the scrutiny trigger cannot turn on that formal label. Pragmatically, we can preserve workable local fee systems by recognizing that generally applicable, evidence-based schedules and state-law regimes may often supply the nexus/proportionality proof—without letting them displace the federal constitutional floor.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent point remains workability/federalism—that applying Nollan/Dolan to generally applicable, legislatively set impact fees risks turning federal courts into overseers of local finance—but that concern goes to how nexus and proportionality are proven, not whether the Takings Clause inquiry is triggered when a fee is imposed as a condition of a specific permit. Chief Justice Roberts’s observation is decisive on the doctrinal coherence: a categorical legislative exemption would hand governments an obvious roadmap to evade Koontz by simply codifying the same permit leverage in an ordinance. Justice Thomas is also right that nothing in the Takings Clause’s text or our Nollan/Dolan/Koontz line makes heightened scrutiny turn on the identity of the decisionmaker, and atextual carveouts are especially suspect where they invite easy circumvention. To preserve administrability, the narrower middle-ground we’ve discussed—applying Nollan/Dolan to permit-conditioned fees while allowing governments to rely on generally applicable studies and state-law schemes as evidence of rough proportionality—best fits the precedents and mitigates the practical disruption respondent fears.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that generally applicable, legislatively set impact fees look like ordinary taxes and so should get only rational-basis review—fails because it elevates form over the Takings Clause’s command: the constitutional problem is leveraging a land-use permit to exact property without just compensation, and Koontz makes clear that money is not categorically different. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, a legislative carveout would hand governments an easy roadmap to evade Nollan/Dolan by codifying the same demands in an ordinance, and nothing in the text or our precedents makes scrutiny turn on the identity of the decisionmaker. Justice Thomas’s emphasis that the Constitution contains no “legislative exception” reinforces that administrability concerns may affect how nexus and rough proportionality are proven, not whether the inquiry is triggered. I therefore remain with petitioner, while agreeing with Roberts and Kagan that the holding can be framed narrowly to avoid destabilizing routine taxation and to leave calibration of proportionality for fee schedules largely to as-applied litigation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that a generally applicable, legislatively set impact fee is functionally a tax and should be insulated from Nollan/Dolan to avoid federal-court supervision of local finance—has force, but it proves too much because it would create the very loophole Koontz guards against. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the constitutional injury arises from leveraging the permitting power over a specific parcel to exact property (including money), and shifting the demand into an ordinance does not eliminate that coercive dynamic; it would instead furnish an easy end-run around precedent. Justice Kagan’s point is the administrability answer: general applicability should affect how nexus and rough proportionality are demonstrated (e.g., through standardized studies), not whether the Takings Clause inquiry is triggered at all. Under an institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, the narrow path is to hold Nollan/Dolan can apply to permit-conditioned fees even when legislatively authorized, while leaving governments room to justify schedules and preserving reliance interests through as-applied proportionality analysis.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that legislatively prescribed, generally applicable impact fees are functionally taxes and therefore categorically outside Nollan/Dolan—fails on the text and our cases: the Takings Clause does not turn on the identity of the decisionmaker, and Koontz’s focus on leveraging a permit to obtain property would be trivially evaded by codifying the demand in an ordinance. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow holding is most persuasive institutionally and doctrinally: we can recognize that Nollan/Dolan may apply to permit-conditioned monetary exactions even when legislatively authorized, while leaving administrability and the calibration of “rough proportionality” to as-applied challenges where general applicability can be relevant to proof. Justice Kagan’s point usefully answers the workability concern: general applicability affects how nexus and proportionality are demonstrated, not whether constitutional scrutiny is triggered in the first place. Nothing raised in conference identifies precedent that compels a legislative carveout, so my vote remains with petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—workability and democratic-accountability, treating legislatively set impact fees like taxes—does not eliminate the unconstitutional-conditions concern when the fee is imposed as the price of a specific land-use permit, and a categorical carveout would create the loophole Chief Justice Roberts identifies. Koontz is decisive for me because it locates the constitutional injury in the leveraging dynamic in the permitting process rather than the form of the exaction, so shifting the demand into an ordinance does not neutralize the Fifth Amendment problem. Justice Kagan’s point also matters under my pragmatic methodology: general applicability can sensibly affect how the government proves nexus and rough proportionality (e.g., through standardized studies), but it should not categorically foreclose scrutiny. A narrow holding—Nollan/Dolan applies to permit-conditioned fees even if legislatively authorized, with proportionality assessed in application—promotes procedural fairness while preserving workable local financing tools tied to actual impacts.

John Roberts.reasoning: Koontz held that the unconstitutional-conditions framework of Nollan and Dolan applies when the government conditions a land-use permit on surrendering property, and it extended that principle to monetary exactions because the leveraging risk is the same. Drawing a categorical line that exempts generally applicable, legislatively set impact fees would invite easy circumvention of Nollan/Dolan by re-labeling permit conditions as “legislative,” undermining the Takings Clause’s protection and producing arbitrary distinctions. A narrow, institutionally cautious resolution is to hold only that Nollan/Dolan can apply to a permit-condition fee even if authorized by ordinance, without deciding the precise degree of tailoring required for all fee regimes or displacing state-law frameworks like California’s Mitigation Fee Act. That approach respects federalism and precedent while preserving constitutional limits on permit leverage.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s text does not distinguish between “legislative” and “ad hoc” conditions; it forbids the government from taking private property for public use without just compensation, and the unconstitutional-conditions doctrine bars accomplishing that result by conditioning a permit on surrendering property. Nollan and Dolan require an essential nexus and rough proportionality when the government leverages permitting to exact property, and Koontz confirms those limits apply to monetary exactions demanded as a permit condition, rejecting the notion that governments may evade scrutiny by converting takings into payments. A generally applicable fee schedule may be a policy choice, but if it operates as a condition on the right to build and is untethered to the project’s impacts, it risks shifting public burdens onto individual owners in a manner inconsistent with the Fifth Amendment’s original public meaning. Accordingly, the County must at least satisfy Nollan/Dolan scrutiny notwithstanding California’s Mitigation Fee Act framework.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause, applied through the Fourteenth Amendment, does not distinguish between “legislative” and “ad hoc” permit conditions when the government conditions issuance of a land-use permit on surrendering property (including money) as an unconstitutional condition. Koontz extended Nollan/Dolan to monetary exactions demanded in the permitting process precisely because of the risk that the government will leverage its permitting power to obtain value lacking an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” to the project’s impacts, and that risk is not eliminated merely because a fee is set by ordinance rather than by a case-by-case official. Allowing a categorical legislative carveout would invite evasion of Nollan/Dolan by relabeling exactions as generally applicable fees, undermining the practical protections those cases provide to property owners. Accordingly, the County’s traffic impact fee, imposed as a condition of a building permit, should be subject to Nollan/Dolan scrutiny as applied.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Koontz held that the Takings Clause’s unconstitutional-conditions doctrine for permit exactions extends beyond dedications of real property to include monetary exactions demanded as a condition of a land-use permit, 570 U.S. 595, 604–05 (2013). Allowing a categorical carveout for fees labeled “legislative” would create an obvious evasion of Nollan’s “essential nexus” and Dolan’s “rough proportionality” requirements, undermining the practical protections those cases provide for ordinary property owners facing permit leverage, Nollan v. Cal. Coastal Comm’n, 483 U.S. 825 (1987); Dolan v. City of Tigard, 512 U.S. 374 (1994). That does not mean every generally applicable fee is unconstitutional; it means the government must be able to show, at least in some administrable way, that the amount demanded is connected to and not grossly out of proportion to the impacts of the permitted development, rather than shifting broad public burdens onto a single applicant. State-law “reasonable relationship” schemes like California’s Mitigation Fee Act may often satisfy that requirement, but they cannot displace the federal constitutional floor when a fee is imposed as a permit condition.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Nollan and Dolan apply the Takings Clause’s unconstitutional-conditions doctrine to permit exactions because conditioning a land-use permit on surrendering property (or its monetary equivalent) risks leveraging the permitting process to obtain what would otherwise require just compensation. Koontz extended that framework to monetary exactions and emphasized the “direct link” between the government’s demand and a specific parcel, a concern that is not categorically eliminated merely because a fee is set by legislation rather than imposed ad hoc. A legislative schedule may make administration more workable, but it cannot supply the essential nexus and rough proportionality that Nollan/Dolan require when the fee is demanded as the price of a permit for a particular project. The Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause therefore calls for Nollan/Dolan scrutiny of such permit-conditioned impact fees, with the general applicability of the fee going to how the government proves proportionality, not whether the doctrine applies at all.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Takings Clause and the unconstitutional-conditions doctrine do not turn on whether the government’s demand is labeled “legislative” or “administrative”; what matters is that a property owner must surrender money or property as a condition of receiving a land-use permit. Nollan and Dolan require an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” to restrain government from leveraging the permitting power to extract value unrelated to the proposed use, and Koontz extended that scrutiny to monetary exactions, emphasizing the risk inherent in permit leverage rather than the identity of the decisionmaker. Allowing a categorical legislative exception would invite circumvention of these constitutional limits by shifting exactions into generally applicable fee schedules, undermining the separation-of-powers duty of courts to enforce the Constitution’s text and history. California’s Mitigation Fee Act “reasonable relationship” standard cannot displace the federal constitutional baseline where a permit is conditioned on an exaction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Nollan and Dolan establish that when the government conditions a land-use permit on the surrender of property interests, the condition must satisfy the Takings Clause’s unconstitutional-conditions limits—an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality.” Koontz extended that framework to monetary exactions demanded in connection with permit approval and did not make heightened scrutiny turn on whether the demand was labeled “legislative” or imposed ad hoc; tying scrutiny to that formal distinction would invite easy evasion and undermine the workability of the doctrine. History and tradition recognize special constitutional suspicion for permit-linked demands that leverage the permitting power, and applying Nollan/Dolan to generally applicable impact fees is a practicable, administrable rule that preserves the constitutional baseline while leaving legislatures room to set fees so long as they are proportionate to development impacts. State-law “reasonable relationship” statutes (e.g., California’s Mitigation Fee Act) may be relevant evidence but cannot displace the federal constitutional standard under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Takings Clause, applied through the Fourteenth Amendment, bars government from leveraging the permitting power to obtain property (including money demanded in exchange for permit approval) without just compensation, and Nollan and Dolan supply the governing unconstitutional-conditions framework requiring an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality.” Koontz extended that framework to monetary exactions and did not adopt a categorical carveout for fees set by legislation, so limiting Nollan/Dolan to ad hoc, discretionary conditions would invite evasion by shifting the same demands into generally applicable schedules. Nothing in the text of the Fifth Amendment turns on whether the condition is imposed by an administrator or a legislature; the relevant question is whether the permit is conditioned on surrendering property in a way that functions as a taking. Precedent remains central, and the best reading of Nollan/Dolan/Koontz is that heightened scrutiny applies to permit-conditioned exactions regardless of their legislative or administrative source, while leaving governments room to justify fees through project-impact-based proportionality.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Koontz v. St. Johns River Water Mgmt. Dist., the unconstitutional-conditions framework of Nollan/Dolan extends to monetary exactions demanded as a condition of permit approval, because the constitutional injury turns on leveraging the permitting power over a specific parcel rather than the form of the demand. Exempting generally applicable, legislatively set impact fees from Nollan/Dolan would create an easily administrable but constitutionally significant loophole, allowing governments to evade heightened scrutiny simply by codifying exactions in fee schedules while still conditioning the right to build on payment. Applying nexus and rough proportionality review to the permit condition here promotes procedural fairness by requiring a demonstrable connection between the fee and the impacts of the proposed development, without dictating policy outcomes or precluding reasonable cost-spreading. The Fifth Amendment Takings Clause, as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment, thus requires at least Nollan/Dolan scrutiny when a building permit is conditioned on payment tied to development impacts, even if set by ordinance.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Takings Clause requires Nollan/Dolan “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” scrutiny for permit conditions imposing legislatively set, generally applicable monetary fees (development impact fees), not just ad hoc, individualized exactions.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Fifth Amendment Takings Clause (as applied to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment), specifically the unconstitutional-conditions doctrine for land-use exactions under Nollan/Dolan and its extension to monetary exactions discussed in Koontz.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Sheetz argues that a county’s demand for money as a condition of a building permit is an exaction that triggers heightened constitutional scrutiny under Nollan and Dolan (as extended by Koontz), and that the Constitution does not allow a government to avoid that scrutiny simply by setting the fee through legislation and applying it broadly; otherwise, governments could impose disproportionate, coercive fees that function like takings while evading meaningful judicial review.
case_analysis.respondent_position: El Dorado County argues that Nollan/Dolan should be limited to discretionary, ad hoc, parcel-specific exactions and not extend to generally applicable, legislatively prescribed development fees; it contends that California’s statutory scheme (including the Mitigation Fee Act’s “reasonable relationship” requirements) already supplies the proper test and review mechanism for such fees, and that applying Nollan/Dolan to broadly applicable fees would constitutionalize routine cost-spreading policy choices and disrupt land-use planning.

San Remo Hotel L.P. v. City and County of San Francisco (Cal. 2002)
Usery v. Turner Elkhorn Mining Co. (1976)
San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court (Cal. 1996)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Sotomayor rightly press the institutional/workability concern that Nollan/Dolan arose from discretionary, parcel-specific bargaining and should not become a roving federal audit of ordinary fiscal policy. But Koontz’s anti-circumvention rationale, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, is that the constitutional problem is the use of permitting leverage to exact value that would otherwise require compensation; making scrutiny turn on whether the condition is codified in an ordinance invites form-based evasion and drains the doctrine of force. I would therefore reject only a categorical legislative carveout while underscoring that governments may satisfy nexus and rough proportionality through legislative impact studies and standardized methodologies, and I would remand for application in the first instance—narrow grounds that preserve administrability and institutional legitimacy. State-law “reasonable relationship” review, though salutary (Justice Alito), cannot displace the federal constitutional floor in unconstitutional-conditions cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest counter: that Nollan/Dolan should be confined to discretionary, ad hoc bargaining to avoid federal courts policing ordinary fiscal legislation. But the Takings Clause’s text contains no carveout for “legislative” conditions, and an original public-meaning approach cannot make the constitutional protection depend on the government’s chosen form when the substance is the same—conditioning a land-use permit on surrendering property (or money in lieu). Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch correctly identify the evasion problem: if general applicability immunizes exactions, governments can nullify Nollan/Dolan by codifying demands, defeating the unconstitutional-conditions principle. Koontz, while arising in a parcel-specific context as Justice Alito notes, confirms that monetary demands can trigger the doctrine; administrability concerns go to how nexus and proportionality are demonstrated (e.g., through studies), not to whether the Constitution applies at all.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s anti-circumvention point is the strongest case for Petitioner, but it proves too much: it assumes that every legislatively set impact fee is simply an end-run around Nollan/Dolan rather than a distinct, generally applicable revenue measure. Koontz, which Roberts and Thomas invoke, repeatedly ties heightened scrutiny to the unconstitutional-conditions problem in a permitting interaction focused on a specific parcel and the government’s individualized leverage; that rationale does not clearly extend to ordinances that spread infrastructure costs prospectively across a class of developments. Justice Kagan’s administrability answer—reliance on impact studies—concedes that the doctrine would migrate into federal judicial oversight of routine fiscal policy, a practical consequence that counsels restraint absent clear textual or precedential command. Under a textualist view of the Takings Clause, the Constitution guarantees compensation for actual takings; it does not authorize courts to impose a freestanding rough-proportionality regime on ordinary legislative fee schedules where state-law “reasonable relationship” constraints already operate.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s anti-circumvention point is the strongest: a categorical “legislative” exemption could invite governments to repackage coercive, parcel-specific demands into ordinances. But that argument assumes legislative schedules replicate the individualized leveraging dynamic that made Nollan/Dolan necessary, whereas routine impact-fee regimes—typically grounded in generally applicable cost-allocation and subject to state-law “reasonable relationship” review—operate more like broad fiscal policy than ad hoc unconstitutional conditions. Koontz, as Justice Alito notes, repeatedly tethered heightened scrutiny to a direct link to a specific parcel in a permitting context, and I am not persuaded it compels extending rough-proportionality review to all legislatively set fees at the risk of federal courts becoming super-legislatures over infrastructure financing. If a future case shows clear legislative circumvention targeted at an identified owner or parcel, I would address that directly; this record does not justify a constitutional rule that destabilizes democratically accountable funding mechanisms with predictable downstream harms to communities that depend on them.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s workability warning is the best point for the Respondent: Nollan/Dolan emerged from ad hoc bargaining, and courts shouldn’t become super-legislatures over ordinary revenue measures. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that a categorical legislative carveout would make constitutional protection turn on drafting form, inviting easy evasion of Koontz’s anti-circumvention logic whenever an exaction can be prepackaged in an ordinance. The administrability concern can be handled at the evidentiary/application stage—allowing legislatures to rely on impact studies and standardized methodologies to show nexus and rough proportionality—rather than by eliminating Nollan/Dolan scrutiny altogether for generally applicable permit conditions. Justice Alito’s reliance on state-law “reasonable relationship” review cannot substitute for the federal unconstitutional-conditions floor, which (textually and pragmatically) should not vary with the government’s choice of decisionmaking procedure.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability worry—that applying Nollan/Dolan to generally applicable fees drags courts into fiscal policy—deserves respect, but it cannot justify a form-based carveout the Fifth Amendment’s text does not supply. Koontz’s anti-circumvention logic targets the government’s use of permit leverage to obtain property value it could not exact outright without satisfying the Takings Clause, and that leverage is present whether the condition is announced by an official or enacted by ordinance; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas note, exempting “legislative” exactions invites easy evasion. The proper separation-of-powers answer is not to dilute the constitutional standard, but to apply it with attention to proof—allowing legislatures to rely on impact studies and standardized methodologies to show nexus and rough proportionality rather than turning judges into rate-setters. Justice Sotomayor’s point about state-law “reasonable relationship” review may mitigate harms, but it cannot displace the federal constitutional floor when a permit is conditioned on surrendering property (including money).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the best point for the Respondent: Nollan/Dolan’s rough-proportionality inquiry can look like judicial supervision of ordinary legislative finance. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Koontz’s anti-circumvention logic would be gutted by a categorical “legislative fee” carveout—governments could immunize the same permit leverage simply by codifying it, making constitutional protection turn on form rather than substance. The way to respect institutional limits is not to exempt generally applicable schedules, but to issue a narrow holding that general applicability is not dispositive and to allow nexus/proportionality to be shown through legislative findings and impact studies on remand. State-law “reasonable relationship” review, as Justice Alito notes, is helpful but cannot replace the federal unconstitutional-conditions floor when permit approval for a specific parcel is conditioned on payment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point—administrability and the risk of constitutionalizing routine fiscal policy—deserves weight, but it cannot justify a categorical exemption keyed to the government’s choice of legislative form. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Koontz’s anti-evasion rationale would be hollow if a jurisdiction could immunize what is functionally a parcel-specific permit condition by embedding the demand in an ordinance; original public meaning and our unconstitutional-conditions cases do not turn on that formal distinction. Workability concerns go to application, not coverage: courts can permit governments to satisfy nexus and rough proportionality through legislative findings and impact studies, and we can remand rather than adjudicate proportionality in the first instance. State-law “reasonable relationship” review, while salutary, cannot displace the federal constitutional floor when permit approval is conditioned on surrendering property or money tied to the proposed development.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—the risk that extending Nollan/Dolan to generally applicable fee schedules would destabilize ordinary infrastructure finance and drag federal courts into rate-setting—deserves real weight as a practical-consequences matter. But Koontz, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, frames the constitutional harm as permit leverage extracting value tied to a specific parcel; making scrutiny turn on whether the demand is enacted by ordinance or imposed ad hoc invites easy circumvention and undermines procedural fairness for similarly situated applicants. The administrability concern can be handled pragmatically at the merits stage by permitting governments to satisfy nexus and rough proportionality through legislative impact studies and standardized methodologies, rather than by creating a categorical “legislative fee” carveout. State-law “reasonable relationship” review, while helpful as Justice Alito notes, cannot substitute for the federal unconstitutional-conditions floor when a permit for a specific project is conditioned on payment.

John Roberts.reasoning: Nollan and Dolan establish that when the government conditions a land-use permit on surrendering property, the Takings Clause requires an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” to the project’s impacts to prevent circumvention of the just-compensation requirement through unconstitutional conditions. Koontz extended that framework to monetary exactions demanded as permit conditions, reasoning that the constitutional injury turns on leveraging the permit to obtain value the government could not take outright without compensation, and it did not recognize a categorical legislative carveout. A narrow, institution-protective holding is that the fee’s legislative and generally applicable character does not, by itself, exempt it from Nollan/Dolan scrutiny; whether this particular fee satisfies nexus and proportionality can be addressed on remand. This approach respects precedent and avoids creating an easy evasion channel whereby governments could relabel individualized exactions as generally applicable fees to escape meaningful Takings Clause review.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Takings Clause, by its text, bars the government from obtaining property (including money as a substitute for a property interest) as the price of a permit unless the condition is tied to the proposed land use; that is the unconstitutional-conditions rule articulated in Nollan and Dolan. Nothing in the Fifth Amendment’s text or original public meaning suggests a carveout when the government accomplishes the same coercive exchange through a generally applicable legislative fee rather than an ad hoc demand, and Koontz confirms that monetary exactions can trigger Nollan/Dolan scrutiny when imposed as a permit condition. Allowing legislatures to evade the “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” requirements would elevate form over substance and invite circumvention of constitutional limits by relabeling exactions as broadly applicable fees. State-law “reasonable relationship” review (e.g., under California’s Mitigation Fee Act) cannot displace the federal constitutional standard when the government conditions a permit on surrendering property.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Nollan and Dolan were crafted to police the risk of coercion and abuse that arises from discretionary, ad hoc permitting decisions tied to a specific parcel, requiring an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” when government uses permitting leverage to exact property interests. Koontz extended that doctrine to monetary demands, but emphasized the “direct link between the government’s demand and a specific parcel of real property” and did not purport to constitutionalize generally applicable, legislatively set fee schedules that operate as ordinary cost-spreading measures. Treating broadly applicable impact fees as Nollan/Dolan exactions would invite federal courts to second-guess routine legislative judgments and would have destabilizing practical consequences for land-use administration, particularly where state law (e.g., California’s Mitigation Fee Act) already imposes a “reasonable relationship” constraint. The Takings Clause’s text requires “just compensation” for takings; it does not compel heightened exaction scrutiny for non-discretionary, generally applicable fees absent the individualized leverage concerns that animated Nollan/Dolan.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Nollan and Dolan’s heightened “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” requirements were crafted to police the special coercive risk that arises when a permitting authority uses discretionary, ad hoc leverage over an individual applicant to extract property interests without just compensation. Koontz extended that framework to certain monetary exactions, but it repeatedly tied the doctrine’s justification to a “direct link” to a specific parcel and the permitting agency’s discretionary bargaining posture, leaving substantial ambiguity about whether the same scrutiny must apply to legislatively set, generally applicable fee schedules. Where a fee is imposed by generally applicable legislation as part of routine cost-spreading, ordinary takings principles and state-law safeguards like California’s Mitigation Fee Act “reasonable relationship” requirements provide a more administrable check without constitutionalizing broad fiscal policy and threatening governments’ ability to fund infrastructure needed for growing communities. Given the practical consequences for local planning and the absence of clear Supreme Court direction extending Nollan/Dolan to legislative impact fees, I would affirm and vote for the County.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Nollan and Dolan ground heightened scrutiny in the unconstitutional-conditions problem created when government leverages the permit process to obtain concessions that would otherwise require just compensation, asking for an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” to the development’s impacts. Koontz extends that logic to monetary exactions, emphasizing the “direct link between the government’s demand and a specific parcel of real property” and the risk of coercion in permitting—concerns that do not disappear merely because the government sets a fee by ordinance rather than by ad hoc negotiation. A categorical legislative carveout would invite easy evasion (relabeling individualized demands as “generally applicable” fees), undermining statutory and doctrinal coherence in the Takings Clause’s permit-condition cases. Workability concerns can be addressed by applying Nollan/Dolan in a manner sensitive to administrable proof (e.g., relying on legislatively developed impact studies), but the constitutional baseline should not turn solely on the lawmaking form.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s protection against unconstitutional conditions does not turn on whether the government labels a permit condition “legislative” or “ad hoc”; what matters is that the government demands money in exchange for permission to use a specific parcel, implicating the same coercive leverage Nollan and Dolan addressed. Koontz held that Nollan/Dolan applies when the government conditions a permit on surrendering property interests, including monetary exactions, because otherwise the Clause could be evaded by substituting cash for a dedication, and nothing in Koontz makes the constitutional rule depend on the source of the condition (ordinance versus administrator). Allowing generally applicable, legislatively set impact fees to escape nexus and proportionality review would invite circumvention and dilute the separation-of-powers function of judicially enforceable constitutional limits on permitting power. Accordingly, Nollan/Dolan scrutiny applies to monetary permit conditions even when imposed pursuant to a generally applicable schedule, with the government bearing the burden to show an essential nexus and rough proportionality to the development’s impacts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Nollan and Dolan apply the Takings Clause’s unconstitutional-conditions doctrine to permit conditions that leverage the permitting process to obtain property (or its equivalent) without just compensation, requiring an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality.” Koontz extended that framework to monetary exactions demanded as a condition of permit approval, emphasizing the “direct link” between the government’s demand and a specific parcel and the risk of leveraging land-use permitting power to obtain disproportionate concessions; that logic does not turn on whether the condition is imposed ad hoc or pursuant to a generally applicable schedule. Allowing governments to evade Nollan/Dolan scrutiny merely by codifying fees in an ordinance would be inconsistent with Koontz’s reasoning and would be impractical and unworkable, inviting circumvention and uneven constitutional protection. Consistent with history, tradition, and precedent, legislatively set impact fees imposed as permit conditions should be subject to Nollan/Dolan when they operate as exactions tied to a particular development approval.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s original public meaning prohibits the government from conditioning a land-use permit on surrendering property (including money demanded in lieu of a property interest) unless the condition is tied to mitigating the project’s impacts; the unconstitutional-conditions doctrine does not turn on whether the demand is imposed ad hoc or by generally applicable legislation. Nollan and Dolan require an “essential nexus” and “rough proportionality” between the permit condition and the proposed development’s effects, and Koontz extended that framework to monetary exactions because the constitutional injury arises from leveraging the permitting power to exact value connected to a specific parcel, not from the formality of the government’s decisionmaking process. Allowing legislatively set impact fees to evade Nollan/Dolan would invite the same evasion Koontz warned against—accomplishing through permit leverage what would otherwise require just compensation—while leaving States free to administer such fees so long as they satisfy the nexus and proportionality limits. Precedent is not to be read as creating a legislative carveout absent clear textual or doctrinal footing, and Koontz’s rationale is best understood as applying to permit conditions demanding money regardless of general applicability.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Koontz v. St. Johns River Water Mgmt. Dist., 570 U.S. 595 (2013), confirms that the unconstitutional-conditions framework of Nollan and Dolan applies when the government conditions a land-use permit on the surrender of a property interest, including demands for money tied to the permit process, because the coercive leverage is the same. Limiting Nollan/Dolan to ad hoc, discretionary exactions would create an administrability loophole—allowing governments to evade meaningful Takings Clause scrutiny simply by legislating fees—undermining procedural fairness for permit applicants and inviting disproportionate burdens without individualized justification. While generally applicable impact-fee regimes may be legitimate tools of planning, the Fifth Amendment (as incorporated through the Fourteenth) requires at least nexus and proportionality review when a monetary condition is imposed as the price of a permit, so that cost-spreading does not become uncompensated taking by another name. State-law “reasonable relationship” review (e.g., California’s Mitigation Fee Act) may be relevant on remand, but it cannot displace the federal constitutional floor established by Nollan/Dolan as extended in Koontz.
